rules.plain_language_rule: Nutrition is a major determinant of training adaptation, recovery, body composition, and performance.
Nutrition should be individualized according to athlete characteristics, training load, position, goals, and schedule.
Sustained energy balance influences body-mass direction, but short-term bodyweight fluctuations should not be interpreted as pure tissue change.
Carbohydrate availability should be matched to training and competition demands.
Protein supports training adaptation and tissue remodeling and should be adequate across the entire day.
Dietary fat is essential and should not be unnecessarily minimized.
Sports nutrition prescriptions should preferentially use body-mass-relative targets where appropriate rather than relying solely on percentages of calories.
Pre-exercise nutrition should support fuel availability, hydration, and gastrointestinal comfort.
During-exercise carbohydrate should depend on duration, intensity, fueling status, and individual tolerance.
Hydration should be individualized rather than prescribed with one fixed volume for all athletes.
Post-exercise nutrition should begin within a practical recovery period; there is no rigid 45-minute anabolic deadline.
Rapid post-exercise carbohydrate replenishment becomes more important when recovery time before the next demanding session is short.
Nutrition interventions should be evaluated against body composition and actual performance, not bodyweight alone.
Food quality and micronutrient adequacy matter alongside calories and macronutrients.
Coaches may provide general nutrition education but should remain within their professional scope.
Suspected clinical nutrition problems should be referred to appropriately qualified professionals.
Supplement recommendations require anti-doping and contamination safeguards.
The platform should prioritize food-first strategies where practical.

master_rule_source_variants.plain_language_rule: Rugby performance depends on multiple physical qualities, not one fitness quality.
Physical requirements vary by position and playing level.
Training should target gaps between the player’s current profile and required profile.
Bigger, stronger, or leaner is not automatically better; physical development must remain functional.
Strength, power, speed, and endurance must be assessed separately even though they interact.
Training decisions should consider both team requirements and individual requirements.
Lifestyle factors influence readiness, recovery, and adaptation.
Lifestyle monitoring should guide conversation and coaching decisions, not diagnose or judge the athlete.
Nutrition, recovery, and conditioning should all be individualized where practical.
